title: Rome: From Republic to Empire

cards.h: A republic that hated kings ended up with an emperor
cards.b:
Rome began as a small town on the Tiber. Legend says it was founded in 753 BCE by Romulus, who killed his twin Remus. Legend is fun, but the real story is better.

Five centuries later Romans swore they would never again live under a king. Then they did, just with a different name.

Tradition says Rome's last king, Tarquin the Proud, was thrown out in 509 BCE. Romans set up a Republic (res publica, 'public thing'). Two consuls, elected for one year, led the state. A Senate of elders advised. Ordinary citizens (the plebs) won their own officials, the tribunes.

Rome beat its Italian neighbours, then fought Carthage in the Punic Wars (264-146 BCE) and destroyed it. It took Greece, Spain and more.

The spoils enriched a few and ruined many farmers. Rich generals with loyal armies became dangerous. The system strained.

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, then in 49 BCE crossed the Rubicon with his army, an act of war against Rome. He won the civil war and became dictator. On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, senators stabbed him, led by Brutus and Cassius.

Caesar's heir Octavian beat Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus. He never called himself king. He kept the Senate and the offices, but held real power.

This began the Pax Romana, about two centuries of relative peace and prosperity.

At its height under Trajan (117 CE), Rome stretched from Britain to Syria. Roads, aqueducts and one law linked millions. Latin and Greek were everywhere.

But around half the people in Italy might have been enslaved, and gladiator games were mass entertainment. Rome was impressive and brutal at once.

cards.h: What did Caesar's death really look like?
cards.b: Myth 1: Caesar said 'Et tu, Brute?' That line is Shakespeare's (1599). Ancient writers disagree about his last words; Suetonius records one version in Greek.Myth 2: the Caesarean section is named after Caesar's birth. His mother lived long after, and such operations then were nearly always fatal for the mother. The name probably comes from the Latin word for cut.

Roman gold in Tamil lands

Pliny the Elder complained about 77 CE that India drained at least 50 million sesterces a year from Rome. After Augustus annexed Egypt in 30 BCE, ships rode the monsoon from the Red Sea to the Malabar coast.

The main port was Muziris in Kerala, now being dug at Pattanam. At Arikamedu near Pondicherry, Roman wine jars and fine red pottery were found. Hoards of Roman gold and silver coins have been found across the Tamil country.

A Sangam poem describes Yavana ships arriving with gold and leaving with pepper. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek merchant's guide of the 1st century CE, lists the Indian ports and cargoes in detail.

Five things to remember

  1. The Republic began about 509 BCE.
  2. Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BCE.
  3. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE and died in 44 BCE.
  4. Augustus became first emperor in 27 BCE.
  5. Rome and India traded heavily.

Think about it

  • Why do republics fall when armies are loyal to generals?
  • Was Augustus a saviour or a trickster?
